chapter_theme: The enemy within the circle: kin and companions whose hostility is hidden. It is worse than an open foe because it is unseen, it wears a family down slowly, and even a sesame-sized amount of it holds ruin.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads the chapter as about a king's court: why to avoid such enmity (881-882), guarding oneself (883), harm to the king (884-886), harm to his house (887-888), not to dismiss it (889), and the end (890). Several verses only name a family or a person, so that royal frame is his.

881.reading: Even shade and water are bad if they do harm, and the நீர் of one's own people too is bad, if it does harm.
881.nuance: நீர் does double work, as water and as nature: தமர்நீர் is the nature of kin, sitting right next to actual water. Parimelazhagar's kin are specifically the relatives who could become inner enemies, and his illnesses from bad water are quite concrete. Manakkudavar reads நிழல்நீர் as one thing, the water in the shade.

882.reading: Don't fear enemies who are like swords, but fear the bond with enemies who are like kin.
882.nuance: The verse says to fear the தொடர்பு and not the person. Parimelazhagar explains that the danger already lies in the existing bond, the one that has been made, and that open foes can be guarded against because they are known.

883.reading: Fear the enemy within and guard yourself; when you falter, it will cut surely, like the potter's cutter.
883.nuance: A மட்பகை is what the potter uses to take a pot off the wheel. Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's point is that the cut is clean and unnoticed. உலைவிடத்து adds patience, as this enemy doesn't need to attack until you are already down.

884.reading: If an inner enmity of unreformed mind appears, it brings many ills of a circle that has gone bad.
884.nuance: The damage is secondary: it spoils the other relationships. Parimelazhagar's analysis is that the enemy works from within to turn others, the king's trust then fails too, and the whole thing compounds. Kalaignar places the mind that won't reform in the person himself, not in another.

885.reading: If an inner enmity appears that has the form of kinship, it brings many ills that have the form of death.
885.nuance: The verse's two lines balance on முறையான், so the closer the tie, the closer to death.

positions.position: It is about a king: an outwardly related enemy who may kill him, aid outside foes, and erode his ministers.
positions.quote: புறப்பகைத் துணையாய் நின்றே அது தோன்றாமல் கோறல் முதலிய வஞ்சனை செய்தலும்

positions.position: It is about enmity among close relatives in general, who all then suffer.

886.reading: If not-being-one arises among those who are one, it is ever hard to reach not-dying.
886.nuance: The wordplay runs through three lines: ஒன்றாமை, ஒன்றியார், ஒன்றல். Oneness is what is broken and also what is needed. Parimelazhagar's எஞ்ஞான்றும் means even when one is at the peak of power.

887.reading: Though joined like a casket and its lid, a family that has inner enmity is not joined.
887.nuance: The image shows a perfect fit with a seam all the same. The lid and the box remain two objects.

positions.position: The members look united but are not, and will split when an outside enemy comes. He notes other readings with the enmity itself as what doesn't join.
positions.quote: உட்பகையான் மனம் வேறுபட்டமையின், புறப்பகை பெற்றுழி வீற்றுவீற்றாவர் என்பதாம்.

positions.position: The enmity and the family are what fit together, and the lid moves aside for the one who comes to take what's inside, as the insider assists the thief.
positions.quote: செப்பகத் துப் பொருள் வாங்குவார்க்கு மூடி துணையாய் அகன்று நிற்குமதுபோல அகன்று நிற்பரென்றவாறு.

888.reading: As பொன் that is rubbed by a file wears away, a family with inner enmity wears down its strength by rubbing against itself.

positions.position: பொன் is iron, the hard metal worn down by a file, and the insider seems to help while slowly separating people.
positions.quote: அரத்தாற் பொரப்பட்ட இரும்பு போல அதனால் பொரப்பட்டு வலி தேயும்.

positions.position: பொன் is gold, which is polished as it is filed. So inner enmity seems to beautify while it wastes strength.
positions.quote: இஃது உட்பகை அழகு செய்வது போலப் பலத்தைக் கெடுக்கு மென்றது.

889.reading: Though only as small as a split sesame seed, inner enmity has ruin within it.
889.nuance: உள்ளதாம் lets the word play with உட்பகை: the ruin is inside what is inside. Parimelazhagar notes the smallness is relative to a king's greatness, and that the large ruin stays contained until its hour comes.

890.reading: Living with those not in accord with you is like living with a snake inside a hut.
890.nuance: Pope's 'domestic life' narrows what the verse leaves open. It says only 'those not in accord', which could be anyone one lives with. Parimelazhagar's point is about smallness and familiarity: in a confined space with long proximity, the bite is a certainty.

links.note: In 735 the land should be free from உட்பகை, which Parimelazhagar glosses as robbers, slanderers and even wild animals. In 881 the same commentator takes the word as kin. The term shrinks from a realm's internal troubles to a family's, and it hurts more in the smaller frame.

Both use a tiny seed against a huge effect. In 104 a millet-seed favour counts as large as a palmyra to those who understand it, and in 889 a sesame-seed enmity holds complete ruin. Small things turn out to be large in the Kural in both moral directions.

source_issues: 890: Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் ends with a bracketed remark on கண்ணோடாதவர் that fits this verse poorly and has an unmatched '['.
